## Introduction

### The Task
Car accidents can be caused due a multitude of reasons and some conditions make a crash more likely to occur. This report aims to determine which conditions naturally occur together by applying cluster analysis. Cluster analysis groups accidents with similar circumstances such as weather, lighting, and road type to discover a meaningful pattern. In addition to cluster analysis, principle component analysis (PCA) is used to get a more clear visual of the clusters. By using both cluster analysis and PCA, it can be determined how accident conditions relate to each other and figure out scenarios where accidents are more likely to occur. This report will compare hierarchical clustering which determines clustering based off of what looks more similar to k-means which will form however many groups it is told to make.


### The Problem

The data used in this report are recorded by the police in Great Britan. The data set is called "Stats19" and is available at <https://www.data.gov.uk/dataset/cb7ae6f0-4be6-4935-9277-47e5ce24a11f/road-accidents-safety-data>. These tables are linked via a unique accident index. 
Some previous cluster analysis work has been reported at:

- [ Cluster analysis](https://ijirt.org/publishedpaper/IJIRT175966_PAPER.pdf)
- [More cluster analysis](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/357727987_Identification_of_Traffic_Accident_Patterns_via_Cluster_Analysis_and_Test_Scenario_Development_for_Autonomous_Vehicles/fulltext/61dcdc17034dda1b9eebd63d/Identification-of-Traffic-Accident-Patterns-via-Cluster-Analysis-and-Test-Scenario-Development-for-Autonomous-Vehicles.pdf)

  
This data can be split into three main groups. Accident information will include: data and time, location, road type and conditions, weather and lighting, and number of vehicles and casualties. Vehicle information will include type and age, maneuver and direction, and driver age and sex. Casualty information will include who was injured (pedestrian, cyclist, driver, etc.), severity, age, sex, and mode of transport. 


This report will focus on grouping conditions such as number of collisions at mini-roundabout, wet conditions, dark or night time, dry conditions, and in an urban setting and where the most serious casualty is reported as a slight injury. These variables and clustering techniques will determine which series of conditions make is so a car accident is more likely to occur. This information will be useful to tell drivers when to be extra careful or to try to avoid driving at all. 

### Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
This report uses PCA for both hierarchical modeling and k-means. Therefore, it is important to have a good foundational understanding of PCA.


Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a dimension reduction technique that identifies new axes (principal components) which captures the maximum variance in the data set. 

- The first principal component (PC1) is the linear combination of the original variables that explains the largest amount of variance in the dataset.

- The second principal component (PC2) is the perpendicular to PC1 and explains the second largest amount of variance. 

The combination of PC1 and PC2 will capture the majority of the variance found in the original dataset. This is useful for simplifying and visualizing the data. 

The first part of PCA is to center and scale the data. The data is centered by taking the mean of each variable to get a center point, then that point is translated to the origin of the graph. The original data points are also shifted in reference to this centroid. Therefore even though the data moved, it is the exact same relative to each other. In order to scale the data, a linear line of best fit needs to be calculated Where each data point is projected onto this line. The line's slope is based off how it can maximize the variance of these projects, this slope is also known as PC1. Thus PC2 is the slope of the line that is orthagonal to PC1. Each of these principal components corresponds to an eigenvector of the covariance matrix and the amount of variance explained by that component is it's eigenvalue. 

Since the eigenvector is the directions of each component and the eigenvalue is the magnitude, the proportion of variance can be calculated by the eigenvalue divided by the sum of all eigenvalues across every component. This value multiplied by 100 will give a percentage detailing how much of the original dataset's variance is captured by the model. 



## The Data

In order to get an idea of what the data is about, a matrix scatter plot was  produced. Each of the chosen sub-type of collisions has been calculated into normalized proportions. Specifically the data for slight injuries, urban setting, dry weather, night time (dark), raining, accidents occurred at a roundabout, and the total number of data points that were collected have been used in this graphic. 

![](../../data_cache/vignettes/unsupervised_classification/scatterplot.html){width="100%" height="600px"}

The positive relationships within the plot means that there is a positive correlation and those conditions together creates a larger probability of the accident to occur. For example when it is raining and dark out where slippery roads and visibility is at it's lowest. 

Whereas a negative relationship means that those events are more mutually exclusive. For example, accidents when the weather is dry versus when it is raining has a negatively linear relationship.


## Hierarchical Clustering


Hierarchical clustering is a great starting point because it can group similar data points together without having to pre-specify the groupings. Here there is one main "trunk" and then four branches.

![](../../data_cache/vignettes/unsupervised_classification/dendrogram.html){width="100%" height="600px"}


The tree was cut at sensible height which will cut off the branches from the main trunk. This is evident by the hscatter plot below where there are 4 groups left.  This is important for Principal Component Analysis (PCA). 

Below is a PCA scatterplot using the hierarchical clustering. It shows that PC1 and PC2 captures 65% and 31.9% of the original variance respectively. The sum of these percentages will detail how much the model captures the original data. Therefore the hscatter plot has a cumulative variance of 96.9%. This high cumulative variance means that this has maintain most of the data's information and ensures that the plots are meaningful.

## K-Means Clustering
K-means clustering can be broken down to a number of steps. Step 1 is to determine the number of clusters you want there to be, this value is known as ‘K’. Step 2 is to take three randomly selected data points. Step 3 is to take the distance of between the first point and the three points that were just selected. Step 4 is to assign each of these random points as a cluster then take the remaining points and assign them to their nearest cluster. Step 5 calculates the mean of each cluster. K-means will repeat this with different starting points until the clusters no longer change. 

‘K’ can be determined by trial and error until the variation is fully reduced. This is where reduction in variance over the number of clusters charts can be handy in determining at which ‘K’ is the most optimal by finding the elbow in the plot, as seen below. It is not advised to have a ‘K’ value that is too high because it will hide natural groupings and will over fit the data. 

![](../../data_cache/vignettes/unsupervised_classification/kvalue.html){width="100%" height="600px"}

The k-means clustering in this report has grouped the accident cases into 4 (k=4). The plot does not show a clear 'elbow' however at k=4, the slope is less dramatic than before then, in addition, it is not wise to over fit the data so having 4 clusters is a safe choice. 

K-means is extremely good at finding natural groups in unlabeled data and is able to discover patterns within complex datasets. First, looking at the centroids will provide insights into the groupings. Below is the first centroids bar cart where it can be clearly seen that cluster 3 has more points in its group than any other cluster. This shows that there is a driving condition that see far more car accidents than any other grouping. 


![](../../data_cache/vignettes/unsupervised_classification/kcentroids1.html){width="100%" height="600px"}


In addition, there is a second centroids bar chart that further breaks down the groupings based off of various variables. This is where the groupings can be better compared since the y-axis has be normalized. It can be seen that cluster 3 predominately pertains to minor accidents that took place in an urban setting. Where as cluster 2 also pertains to more main accidents but not in an urban setting.

![](../../data_cache/vignettes/unsupervised_classification/kcentroids2.html){width="100%" height="600px"}


K-means clustering analysis will create it's own PC1 and PC2 values. The scatter plot below demonstrates this. K-means model's PC1 and PC2 captures 48.5% and 38% of the variance from the original data. Therefore the cumulative variance is 86.5%. This is still a high cumulative variance however it does capture less of the data than the hierarchical clustering Thus, in this case, k-means is less accurate than its hierarchical  counterpart
